# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
I've read the comment carefully and checked its numbers. Its forensic sections (1–5) are valuable. Several of them confirm, with microdata, problems I could only infer from the Halden working paper:
- Hours fell by less than the schedule implied.
- The revenue figure is nominal.
- Gains appear in every sector partly because dividing by 0.8 guarantees them.

The comment then goes well beyond its evidence. Its central conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", is contradicted by its own corrected estimate. It is also contradicted by the Varden trial, which the comment cites selectively.

## What holds up

Most of the arithmetic checks out:
- Table 1: 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8.
- Hours: 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%); 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%).
- Table 2 rows: 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8%.
- Revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, which is −2.6% in real terms.

The attrition finding is the most important new fact. If seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, and six cited workload or output, then the working paper's description ("withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons") is materially wrong. That deserves a direct response from the Halden authors. The comment should say whether they were contacted.

The finding that 19 of 23 manager indices exceeded the record-based index is also persuasive evidence of systematic upward bias in the primary outcome.

## Major issues

**1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own evidence.**
- After the two corrections the authors actually made (record-based output and actual hours), a gain of +10.8% per actual hour remains.
- The Varden trial finds +12.5% per actual hour in case-processing (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That trial already has most of the features the comment recommends: randomisation, record-based output, actual hours from timesheets, and analysis that doesn't depend on who volunteered. Only the long follow-up is missing.

The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature", yet doesn't mention that the same trial's case-processing stratum shows a per-hour gain that survives every correction except duration. You can't treat Varden as authoritative for the negative result and ignore its positive one.

The defensible conclusion is much narrower: Halden overstated the gain by roughly half, and no study yet shows whether the remainder lasts. That is not the same as "entirely an artifact".

**2. The comment's wording escalates from section to section.**

| Where | Claim |
|---|---|
| Abstract, first claim | the problems "account for most of the reported gain" |
| Section 6 | the residual is "plausibly" novelty |
| Abstract and conclusion | gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" |
| Data note | corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole" |

The conclusion then generalises from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" as a class. Each step is stronger than the one before, and the last one contradicts the authors' own data note.

**3. Attrition is described but never corrected.** The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems, and attrition is the first. But Table 2 corrects only the output measure and hours. The withdrawn organisations appear in no calculation. If any of the seven that started the schedule submitted monthly indices before leaving, include them on an intention-to-treat basis. Otherwise, give bounds: assume plausible outcomes for the nine, or use Lee-style bounds. Without that, attrition supports the direction of bias but not its size.

**4. Table 2 mixes different subsets of organisations.** The rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. So the move from +23.4% to +10.8% combines the effect of each correction with differences between the groups. Run all four specifications on the same 17 organisations (manager index with scheduled hours, record-based with scheduled, and so on). That would separate how much comes from the output measure and how much from the hours measure.

**5. The breakdown of extra hours doesn't add up.** The logs show the four remaining days got 0.7 hours longer and 1.6 hours were worked on the day off. Taking the 32 scheduled hours as the base:

> 32 + (4 × 0.7) + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**

The reported actual figure is **34.6**. Measuring from baseline actual days (8.06 hours) makes the gap worse, at about 36.6. The difference is around two hours a week. Either the components are measured on different bases (for example, averaged only over employees who extended their days), or something reduces hours elsewhere, such as leave or holidays. Since the hours correction carries much of the argument, the authors should reconcile these figures.

**6. Novelty is assumed when it could be tested.**
- The Halden microdata include **monthly** output indices. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should rise and then fall across months 1–6. The authors have the data to check this and didn't.
- They rely instead on a self-reported energy measure, which is not output.
- Even that extrapolation is shaky. A straight line through two points (0.61 at month 3, 0.29 at month 6) reaches zero at about month **8.7**, not "around month ten". A straight line is also an arbitrary assumption; the decline could level off.
- The claim that "the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is rhetoric, not evidence. The honest position is that the six-month data can't tell the two explanations apart.

**7. The comment misdescribes Varden's meetings analysis, and is more sceptical of it than of its own novelty account.**
- *How it was presented.* The Varden authors did not offer meetings as an established mechanism. They wrote that "a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism", labelled the analysis unregistered, and registered a confirmatory test for 24 months.
- *How it was collected.* The comment says the data were "selected for analysis after the results were known". In fact they were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The seven offices are simply all the treated case-processing offices.
- *What is fair.* It is fair to warn others against citing meetings as a mechanism. My own earlier concern also still stands: there is no baseline for meeting hours, so "offices that cut meetings most" can't actually be computed.
- *Different standards.* The comment dismisses meetings, which rest on seven offices and are consistent with Halden's interviews (47 of 58 managers mentioned meetings). Yet it adopts novelty on two time points of a self-reported measure. The same scepticism should apply to both.

**8. The record-based output measure may have its own downward bias.** Some organisations' records were "billable hours delivered". For those, output falls automatically when hours fall, so the measure can't show a per-hour gain even if one exists. Show the manager-versus-records gap separately by type of record (billable hours, tickets, units, cases). If the gap is concentrated among the billable-hours organisations, part of the −3.8 points reflects the measure, not manager optimism.

## Smaller points

- **Deflator.** Consumer prices are a rough deflator for business revenue. Sector-specific producer price indices would be better, and inflation adjustment means little for non-profits. Real revenue also needs comparing with similar non-participating organisations, since many firms may have seen real declines over the same period.
- **Retail.** The −11.2% for retail and hospitality rests on three organisations. It points the same way as the manager-reported −6.9%, but it is not an estimate in its own right.
- **Varden's counter result is less certain than described.** As noted in my review of Varden, its counter stratum has 5 offices per arm with clustered standard errors, so its confidence intervals are probably too narrow. The direction is credible, but calling it "the most reliable finding to date" overstates its precision. It is also public counter work, not retail.
- **The data note** is good practice. Its caveat should appear in the abstract, which currently presents +10.8% as if it applied to the whole pilot.

## Suggested revisions

1. Change the conclusion to match the evidence. For example: "Correcting for measurement roughly halves the reported gain, to about 11% in the subset with usable data. Whether the remainder is durable cannot be determined from a six-month pilot."
2. Bound the effect of attrition, and compute all four Table 2 specifications on the same 17 organisations.
3. Reconcile the breakdown of extra hours with the 34.6-hour total.
4. Test novelty directly using the monthly output indices.
5. Engage with Varden's case-processing result, and correct the description of its meetings analysis.

Taken together, the three documents point to a consistent picture:
- Uncontrolled pilots measured against scheduled hours roughly double the apparent gain.
- In coverage-bound work, reduced hours cost output and service.
- In backlog-style work, a per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% survives the better corrections.
- How durable that gain is remains open, and the 24-month Varden follow-up is the most likely evidence to settle it.

I can draft a reply to the comment, or a short synthesis note setting out the three studies' estimates side by side.
